questions.question: What do the HTTP Cache-Control and ETag headers do, and how do they affect caching behavior in browsers and CDNs?
questions.answer: Cache-Control controls freshness — how long a response can be reused without checking back with the origin at all. Directives include max-age (how long the browser can cache it), s-maxage (a separate, often longer, lifetime for shared caches like CDNs), public/private (whether shared caches are allowed to store it, important for personalized content), no-store (never cache at all — for sensitive data), and no-cache (confusingly, this actually means 'you can store it, but must revalidate before every use,' not 'don't cache'). ETag controls validation — it's an opaque token identifying a specific version of the resource's content. Once a cached response's max-age expires, instead of blindly re-downloading the full resource, the client sends a conditional request with an If-None-Match header containing the stored ETag; if the server's current ETag matches, it replies with a lightweight 304 Not Modified (no body), and the client keeps using its cached copy — saving bandwidth versus a full re-download while still guaranteeing correctness. In practice, browsers, CDNs, and any reverse proxies in the chain each apply the same Cache-Control rules independently, which is why s-maxage (shared caches) and max-age (private/browser cache) are often set differently — a common pattern is a hashed, immutable filename with Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable for static assets (never needs revalidation since the URL itself changes on update), versus a short max-age plus an ETag validator for frequently-updated content like HTML pages or API responses.

questions.question: What is IGMP, and what role does it play in IP multicast group membership?
questions.answer: IGMP (Internet Group Management Protocol) is the signaling protocol that IPv4 hosts and their local routers use to establish and manage multicast group membership on a network segment — it operates at the network layer, similarly to ICMP. When a host wants to receive a multicast stream (say, a live video feed sent to a Class D address in the 224.0.0.0-239.255.255.255 range), it sends an IGMP Membership Report announcing interest in that specific group; the local multicast router tracks which groups have interested members on each attached network and only forwards multicast traffic for groups that actually have subscribers there, rather than flooding it everywhere — this is what makes multicast efficient compared to broadcasting to everyone. Routers periodically send IGMP Membership Queries to check whether members are still present, and (from IGMPv2 onward) hosts can send an explicit Leave Group message to unsubscribe promptly rather than waiting for a query timeout. On switched LANs, IGMP snooping lets switches (which normally have no Layer 3 awareness) listen in on this IGMP traffic to learn which specific ports have multicast subscribers, so they can forward multicast frames only to those ports instead of flooding every port on the VLAN. Note that IGMP itself is IPv4-specific; IPv6 uses the analogous Multicast Listener Discovery (MLD) protocol instead.

questions.question: What security risks exist on open/public WiFi, and how does WPA3 improve on WPA2 in addressing them?
questions.answer: Open (unencrypted) public WiFi and even password-protected WPA2 networks carry real risks: on a fully open network, anyone within range can passively capture all unencrypted traffic; and on WPA2 networks, the four-way handshake used during authentication was found vulnerable to KRACK (Key Reinstallation Attack, 2017), where an attacker manipulates and replays handshake messages to trick a device into reinstalling an already-used encryption key, potentially allowing traffic decryption or injection. Separately, WPA2's pre-shared key (PSK) handshake can be captured by anyone in range and then cracked offline via dictionary/brute-force attacks against weak passwords, entirely without needing to be connected to the network. WPA3 addresses these specifically: it replaces WPA2's handshake with SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals, also called the Dragonfly handshake), which is designed to be resistant to offline dictionary attacks — an attacker who captures the handshake can't productively brute-force it offline the way they could with WPA2. WPA3 also adds forward secrecy, meaning that even if a password is later compromised, previously captured encrypted sessions can't be retroactively decrypted (protecting against 'harvest now, decrypt later' attacks), and it introduces individualized data encryption for open networks (via Opportunistic Wireless Encryption), meaning even unauthenticated public WiFi traffic gets per-device encryption rather than being sent in the clear. Since 2020, WPA3 support has been mandatory for the Wi-Fi Alliance's certification, though many networks still run WPA2/WPA3 'transitional' mode for backward compatibility with older client devices.

questions.question: What is the difference between a DoS attack and a DDoS attack, and what makes DDoS attacks harder to mitigate?
questions.answer: A DoS (Denial of Service) attack originates from a single source — one machine flooding a target with traffic or exploiting a protocol weakness to exhaust its resources and make it unavailable to legitimate users. A DDoS (Distributed Denial of Service) attack is the same goal achieved from many sources simultaneously — typically thousands of compromised devices forming a botnet, all directed by an attacker's command-and-control infrastructure. DDoS is harder to mitigate for several concrete reasons: (1) you can't simply block one IP address, since traffic legitimately arrives from thousands of different, geographically distributed source addresses that individually look like normal users; (2) the aggregate traffic volume a botnet can generate vastly exceeds what any single-source DoS attack could produce, since it's the sum of bandwidth across every compromised device; (3) distinguishing malicious from legitimate traffic becomes much harder at scale — application-layer DDoS attacks (like HTTP floods) can mimic real user request patterns closely enough that simple rate-limiting per IP is ineffective when each IP is only sending a modest, individually 'reasonable' amount of traffic. Effective DDoS mitigation typically requires infrastructure specifically built for this — anycast-distributed scrubbing centers, traffic pattern analysis to detect botnet behavior at aggregate scale, and upstream ISP/CDN collaboration — rather than something a single origin server or basic firewall can reliably handle on its own.

questions.question: Explain how STUN, TURN, and ICE work together to establish peer-to-peer connectivity through NAT, such as in a WebRTC call.
questions.answer: Two devices behind separate NATs generally can't just connect to each other directly, because neither has a publicly routable address that the other can dial — each only knows its own private LAN IP. STUN (Session Traversal Utilities for NAT) solves the simpler part of this: a client sends a request to a public STUN server, which observes the source IP:port that the packet actually arrived from (after the client's NAT rewrote it) and reports that back to the client — this is the client's 'server-reflexive' public address, discovering what the outside world sees. This works well for 'full-cone' or moderately restrictive NATs where the mapping is predictable, but fails for symmetric NAT (common on corporate networks and mobile carriers), where the NAT assigns a different external port for every distinct destination, making the address learned from a STUN server useless for connecting to a different peer. TURN (Traversal Using Relays around NAT) is the fallback for exactly that case: a TURN server acts as a relay that both peers connect to and send traffic through, guaranteeing connectivity at the cost of higher latency and bandwidth cost (all media now flows through a third-party relay instead of directly between peers). ICE (Interactive Connectivity Establishment) is the overall framework that ties this together: each peer gathers a set of address 'candidates' — its local LAN address, its STUN-discovered server-reflexive address, and a TURN relay address as a last resort — exchanges these candidates with the other peer (via a signaling channel, not part of ICE itself), and then performs connectivity checks across all candidate pairs, picking the best one that actually works (preferring direct host-to-host, then STUN-assisted, then falling back to TURN relay only if nothing better succeeds). This is exactly the mechanism WebRTC uses to establish audio/video connections directly between browsers whenever possible.

questions.question: What is BGP hijacking, and how does RPKI/Route Origin Validation help mitigate it?
questions.answer: BGP hijacking occurs when an autonomous system (AS) announces IP prefixes it doesn't actually own or have authorization to route — either maliciously or through misconfiguration — causing other networks that receive and trust that announcement to send traffic for those IP addresses toward the hijacking AS instead of the legitimate owner. Because BGP is fundamentally a trust-based protocol with no built-in verification of who's actually authorized to announce a given prefix, a hijack can succeed simply because the false announcement looks like a normal (often shorter, more specific) route, and BGP's path-selection logic will often prefer it. Consequences range from traffic being silently blackholed (denial of service) to being actively intercepted and inspected or modified before being forwarded on to the real destination (a man-in-the-middle at internet scale) — this has happened in real, documented incidents affecting major providers. RPKI (Resource Public Key Infrastructure) mitigates this by letting the legitimate holder of an IP prefix cryptographically sign a ROA (Route Origin Authorization) — a statement asserting 'AS X is authorized to originate this prefix' — published in a trusted RPKI repository. Routers performing Route Origin Validation (ROV) can check incoming BGP announcements against these signed ROAs and classify each as Valid, Invalid, or Unknown (no ROA published); networks can then configure policy to reject or deprioritize routes marked Invalid, meaning a hijacker announcing someone else's prefix without a matching, correctly-signed ROA gets automatically filtered out by any router doing ROV — though the protection is only as strong as how widely ROV has actually been deployed across the internet's networks, since RPKI doesn't prevent a hijack announcement from propagating through networks that don't perform validation.

questions.question: Explain route summarization and VLSM (Variable Length Subnet Masking), and why they matter in large-scale network design.
questions.answer: VLSM is the practice of using different subnet mask lengths within the same overall network, rather than one fixed mask everywhere (Fixed-Length Subnet Masking). This lets a network designer size each subnet to actually match its real host requirement — a branch office LAN needing 60 hosts gets a /26 (64 addresses), while a point-to-point WAN link between two routers, needing only 2 addresses, gets a /30 — instead of wastefully applying the same large subnet everywhere. Classful routing protocols (like RIPv1) couldn't support this, since they only advertised one mask per network class; VLSM requires classless routing protocols like OSPF, EIGRP, or BGP that carry the subnet mask alongside each route advertisement. Route summarization (supernetting) is essentially the inverse operation at the routing-table level: instead of a router advertising many individual specific routes to its neighbors, it advertises one summarized, less-specific route that covers a contiguous block of those subnets — for example, advertising 192.168.0.0/22 instead of four separate /24 routes. This matters enormously at scale because routing table size directly impacts router memory, CPU for route computation, and the bandwidth/processing cost of routing update exchanges — a large ISP or enterprise network with thousands of subnets would produce unmanageable table sizes and slow convergence without summarization; VLSM is what makes efficient, hierarchical address allocation possible in the first place, and route summarization is what turns that hierarchical structure into compact routing tables. The two work together: careful VLSM design (allocating contiguous address blocks by region/site in a planned, hierarchical way) is what makes clean summarization at higher levels of the network actually possible.

questions.question: What is the bandwidth-delay product, and why does it matter when tuning TCP window sizes on high-latency, high-bandwidth links?
questions.answer: The bandwidth-delay product (BDP) is the amount of data that can be 'in flight' on a network path at any given moment: BDP = bandwidth × round-trip time. For example, a 1 Gbps link with a 100ms RTT has a BDP of about 12.5 MB — that's how much data would need to be unacknowledged and in transit simultaneously to keep the link fully utilized. TCP's original window field is only 16 bits, capping the receive window at 65,535 bytes (64 KB) — fine for the low-latency LANs TCP was designed for in the 1980s, but on a modern high-bandwidth, high-latency ('long fat network') path, that 64 KB ceiling is far smaller than the BDP. When the TCP window is smaller than the path's BDP, the sender exhausts its allowed in-flight data and must stall, waiting for ACKs before sending more — meaning the connection can never actually use the full available bandwidth no matter how fast the link theoretically is, since it's throttled by round-trip latency rather than link capacity. This is exactly why a single large file transfer across a fast intercontinental or satellite link can feel like dial-up: the bottleneck isn't bandwidth, it's window size relative to RTT. The fix, standardized in RFC 1323, is TCP window scaling — a negotiated option (agreed during the SYN handshake, and fixed for the life of the connection) that multiplies the advertised window by a scale factor, allowing effective windows up to roughly 1 GB. In practice, tuning for BDP means ensuring window scaling is enabled and that OS send/receive buffers are sized at least as large as the calculated BDP — undersized buffers leave bandwidth unused, while oversized buffers waste memory and can contribute to bufferbloat (excess queuing delay) under load.

questions.question: How does consistent hashing minimize data or session redistribution when nodes are added or removed from a distributed caching or load-balancing layer, compared to naive modulo-based hashing?
questions.answer: Naive hashing assigns a key to a server using key_hash % N, where N is the current number of servers. The problem is that N appears directly in the formula: if you add or remove even a single server, N changes, and the modulo result for nearly every key changes along with it — meaning almost all keys suddenly map to a different server than before. For a distributed cache, this is catastrophic: it effectively invalidates the entire cache at once (a 'cache stampede'), sending a flood of requests to the origin/database simultaneously as every key needs to be refetched into its new location. Consistent hashing solves this by decoupling key placement from N. Both servers and keys are hashed onto positions on a fixed, circular hash space (a 'ring' — typically 0 to 2^32-1), and each key is assigned to the first server encountered going clockwise from the key's position on the ring. When a server is added, it only takes over the portion of the ring between itself and the next server counter-clockwise — meaning only the keys that fall in that specific arc need to move, while every other key's server assignment is completely unaffected. Removing a server has the same localized effect in reverse: only the keys it was responsible for get reassigned to the next server clockwise. In a system with N servers, adding or removing one server under consistent hashing only remaps roughly 1/N of all keys, versus nearly all keys under modulo hashing. In practice, implementations also use 'virtual nodes' — hashing each physical server to multiple points on the ring — to smooth out load distribution and avoid one server unluckily owning a disproportionately large arc.

questions.question: What is microsegmentation in a zero-trust network architecture, and how does it differ from a traditional perimeter-based security model?
questions.answer: Traditional perimeter security operates on an implicit-trust model: a firewall guards the boundary between 'inside' (trusted) and 'outside' (untrusted), and once traffic is inside the network, it generally moves freely between internal systems with minimal inspection — the network is effectively flat from a security-policy standpoint. This breaks down badly against modern threats and modern architectures: if an attacker compromises even one internal system (via phishing, a vulnerable service, etc.), they can move laterally across the internal network largely unimpeded, since internal ('east-west') traffic was never designed to pass through the same scrutiny as traffic crossing the perimeter. It's also a poor fit for cloud/container environments, where IP addresses are ephemeral, workloads span multiple clouds, and there often isn't a clean network 'perimeter' to defend in the first place. Zero trust rejects the idea that anything should be implicitly trusted based on network location — every request, regardless of whether it originates inside or outside the traditional boundary, must be explicitly authenticated and authorized. Microsegmentation is the mechanism that enforces this at the network level: rather than one large trusted zone, it creates fine-grained security boundaries — often around individual workloads, VMs, containers, or even specific services — with explicit policies dictating exactly which other workloads each one is allowed to communicate with, enforced independent of physical network topology (often via software agents, cloud security groups, or SDN rather than traditional network-address-based firewall rules). The practical benefit is blast-radius containment: even if an attacker compromises one workload, microsegmentation policy prevents them from freely reaching every other system on the network, limiting lateral movement to only the explicitly permitted paths.

questions.question: How can session hijacking occur over a network, and what mechanisms (secure cookies, TLS, token rotation) mitigate it?
questions.answer: After a user authenticates, a web application typically issues a session token (a cookie, JWT, or similar bearer credential) that proves authentication for subsequent requests — whoever possesses that token is treated as that authenticated user, without needing to re-supply a password. Session hijacking is the theft or forging of that token so an attacker can impersonate the victim without ever needing their credentials. Common vectors include: session sniffing — passively capturing unencrypted traffic on a shared network (like open WiFi) to extract the token in transit; cross-site scripting (XSS) — injecting malicious JavaScript into a vulnerable page that reads and exfiltrates the victim's cookie/token, which is currently one of the most common real-world vectors, especially against tokens stored in localStorage (which JavaScript can always read) rather than cookies; session fixation — tricking a victim into using a session ID the attacker already knows before they authenticate, so the attacker's pre-chosen ID becomes valid once login succeeds; and info-stealing malware that scrapes browser cookies directly off a compromised device. Mitigations map to these vectors: TLS/HTTPS encrypts traffic end-to-end, defeating passive network sniffing (though it does nothing once a token is already stolen by other means); the Secure cookie flag ensures the cookie is only ever transmitted over HTTPS; the HttpOnly flag prevents JavaScript from reading the cookie at all, directly blocking XSS-based cookie theft (though tokens deliberately exposed to JavaScript, like many JWT implementations, don't get this protection); regenerating the session ID immediately after login defeats session fixation; and short token lifetimes combined with rotation (issuing a new token periodically, or on sensitive actions, and invalidating the old one) limit how long a stolen token remains useful even if theft does occur. No single mechanism is complete on its own — defense in depth across transport security, cookie flags, and token lifecycle management is what actually closes the various hijacking vectors.

questions.question: Explain how SDN (Software-Defined Networking) separates the control plane from the data plane, and what problems this architecture solves compared to traditional networking.
questions.answer: In traditional networking, every switch and router is a self-contained device combining two functions: the data plane (the actual hardware-accelerated forwarding of packets/frames from an input port to an output port, based on locally stored tables) and the control plane (the logic that decides what those forwarding rules should be — computed independently by each device via routing protocols like OSPF or BGP, or spanning-tree calculations). Because control-plane logic runs independently and locally on every single device, making network-wide policy changes means touching many devices individually, and the network's overall behavior emerges indirectly from many separate, device-local decisions rather than being centrally specified. SDN restructures this by physically separating the two: 'dumb' forwarding devices (switches) retain only the data plane, executing forwarding rules exactly as instructed, while the control plane logic is centralized in a software-based SDN controller that has visibility into and authority over the entire network. The controller communicates with switches via a standardized southbound protocol — OpenFlow being the original and most widely known — to install, modify, and remove flow rules in each switch's forwarding table. This solves several real problems: (1) centralized, programmatic control means network-wide policy changes can be pushed from one place instead of reconfiguring every device individually; (2) it enables rapid, automated response to changing conditions (traffic engineering, load-based rerouting) without manual reconfiguration; (3) it decouples forwarding hardware from control logic, allowing cheaper, simpler, vendor-neutral switches since the intelligence lives in software at the controller. The trade-off is that the controller becomes a critical, centralized dependency — a compromised or unavailable controller has much broader blast radius than a single traditional router failing, which is a genuine security and resilience consideration in SDN deployments.

questions.question: What is a jitter buffer, and how does it compensate for variable network delay in VoIP or real-time streaming applications?
questions.answer: Jitter is the variation in packet arrival delay — because IP networks are best-effort, packets carrying successive chunks of a voice or video stream can each take slightly different amounts of time to arrive, arriving out of their original sending order or bunched together unevenly, even though they were transmitted at a steady, even rate. If those packets were played out to the listener the instant they arrived, this unevenness would produce choppy, robotic-sounding audio or stuttering video. A jitter buffer sits at the receiving end and absorbs this variability: it holds incoming packets briefly, reorders any that arrived out of sequence, and then releases them to the playback device at a smooth, steady rate rather than the network's uneven delivery rate — deliberately trading a small amount of added end-to-end delay for a much smoother, more consistent playback experience. There are two general designs: a static (fixed) jitter buffer holds packets for a constant amount of time regardless of current conditions — simple, but not ideal for links with fluctuating jitter; a dynamic (adaptive) jitter buffer continuously monitors observed jitter and adjusts its buffering depth on the fly, shrinking when the network is stable (minimizing added delay) and growing when jitter increases (avoiding dropped/late packets). This adjustment involves a real trade-off: a larger buffer better tolerates jitter and reduces the odds of a packet arriving too late to be used (which gets discarded, causing an audible gap), but it also adds more fixed latency to the call — for interactive voice, total one-way delay much above ~150ms starts to noticeably hurt conversational quality, so jitter buffer sizing has to balance smoothness against added latency rather than simply maximizing buffer depth.

questions.question: What is MPLS, and how does label switching improve forwarding performance and enable traffic engineering compared to conventional hop-by-hop IP routing?
questions.answer: In conventional IP routing, every router along a packet's path independently performs a full destination-address lookup against its routing table to determine the next hop — this happens at every single hop, even though the packet is following essentially the same route the whole way. MPLS (Multiprotocol Label Switching) changes this: when a packet enters an MPLS network, an ingress Label Edge Router (LER) classifies it into a Forwarding Equivalence Class (FEC) — a group of packets that will be treated identically for forwarding purposes, typically based on destination and other criteria — and attaches a short, fixed-length label representing that FEC. From that point on, every intermediate Label Switch Router (LSR) makes its forwarding decision purely by looking up the label (a simple, fast table index operation) rather than re-parsing the full IP header and performing a longest-prefix-match lookup — the label is swapped for a new one at each hop until the egress LER pops the label and delivers the plain IP packet. Historically, this label-lookup speed was the primary motivation for MPLS (avoiding expensive IP lookups at every hop); with modern hardware-accelerated routers, raw forwarding speed is less of a differentiator, and MPLS today is used mainly for traffic engineering and service capabilities that hop-by-hop IP routing can't easily provide. Specifically, MPLS establishes explicit Label Switched Paths (LSPs) — a predetermined sequence of routers a given traffic class will follow — which lets network operators steer specific traffic along a chosen path (for load distribution, low-latency routing, or avoiding congested links) rather than simply following whatever the IGP's shortest-path calculation independently decides at each hop. This also underpins BGP/MPLS Layer 3 VPNs (letting a single provider's core network carry logically separate customer networks) and enables differentiated QoS treatment per label, both of which are difficult to achieve cleanly with pure destination-based IP routing.
